football_evidence.question: Can Indiana’s pass rush get to Drake Lindsey?
football_evidence.assessment: No material disagreement: EdgeDesk and the line are within 1.5 points.
supporting: When Minnesota has the ball (pass protection against the pass rush): Minnesota’s offense has allowed a sack on 2.5% of its dropbacks, and Indiana’s defense sacks the quarterback on 13.5% of opponent dropbacks (FBS average 5.7%).
When Minnesota has the ball (the run game against the run defense): Minnesota’s offense averages 3.3 yards per carry, and Indiana’s defense allows 3.5 yards per carry (FBS average 5.0).
When Minnesota has the ball (the red zone): Minnesota’s offense succeeds on 31.4% of its red-zone plays, and Indiana’s defense allows success on 32.6% of opponent red-zone plays (FBS average 43.6%).

When Minnesota has the ball (big plays on the ground): Minnesota’s offense turns 3.5% of its runs into explosive gains, and Indiana’s defense gives up explosive gains on 3.8% of opponent runs (FBS average 6.5%).
contradicting: When Indiana has the ball (third down): Indiana’s offense converts 36.0% of its third downs, and Minnesota’s defense allows opponents to convert 30.1% of their third downs (FBS average 39.5%).
In his last two games (Ohio State and Michigan), Hoover averaged 6.5 yards per attempt, against 10.7 in his six games before that.
quarterbacks: Josh Hoover has completed 116 of 186 passes (62.4%) for 1,742 yards, 9.4 yards per attempt, 18 touchdowns and 1 interception in eight games for Indiana, and has been sacked on 10 of 196 dropbacks.

Drake Lindsey has completed 141 of 221 passes (63.8%) for 1,490 yards, 6.7 yards per attempt, 10 touchdowns and 6 interceptions in seven games for Minnesota, and has been sacked on 5 of 226 dropbacks.

model: Indiana’s defense has to come out ahead in the pass-rush matchup: it sacks the quarterback on 13.5% of opponent dropbacks, against an offense that has allowed a sack on 2.5% of its dropbacks.
Indiana’s offense has to hold its own on third down against a defense that allows opponents to convert 30.1% of their third downs.
Indiana’s defense has to come out ahead on long runs: it gives up explosive gains on 3.8% of opponent runs, against an offense that turns 3.5% of its runs into explosive gains.
Indiana’s defense has to come out ahead on the ground: it allows 3.5 yards per carry, against an offense that averages 3.3 yards per carry.
market: Minnesota’s defense has to come out ahead on third down: it allows opponents to convert 30.1% of their third downs, against an offense that converts 36.0% of its third downs.
